# WHAT? the tutorial

### What a SETTLE program is, in the standard terms

A SETTLE model is an Ising-type energy function over binary spins. Each thing is a spin si in , with +1 read as yes. A lean is a field hi and a pull is a coupling Jij: `leans: :yes, by: b` adds +b to hi (and -b for `:no`), `a.pulls :b, by: w` adds +w to Jab, and `pushes` adds -w.

Ask the MCP. pkg It always has the answers to 'what is this?' and 'how do I use this?' For : the docs, the help, the setup on your machine, and the tools for using it.

## Five things one small language does (WHAT IT IS FOR)

## A thing, a lean, a pull, a hold, a settle, an ask (WAT DIS)

A program names its things in a `model` block. Yes is +1 and no is -1 underneath, and every answer SETTLE gives is a count of how often a thing was yes.

The light was on in 88.0% of 40,000 samples. For a lean of 1 the exact answer is (1 + tanh 1) / 2 = 88.08%, so the count is right to within the noise of counting. Move the slider to see the rule for any lean.

A pull of 1 makes two things agree about 88% of the time, the same number as a lean of 1 makes one thing say yes, and for the same reason: the rule inside is one rule. Pulls are also how news travels. Hold one light and its pulls carry what you saw to the others.

Rain leans toward no, so on its own it is yes % of the time. Hold the grass wet and rain becomes yes % of the time. The whole of decisions, further down, is this one word.

A settle first burns in a tenth of its sweeps and throws them away, then keeps one sample per sweep. The seed makes the run repeatable: the same seed gives the same samples every time.

An ask can count a joint event too: `ask :rain, and: :sprinkler` counts the samples in which both were yes. The language reference lists every form.

## The coin rule, sweeps, cooling, counting (HOW DAT)

The temperature T divides the input: the rule is really (1 + tanh(I / T)) / 2. Hot means every coin is nearly fair; cold means every coin follows its input. A p-bit is a device that does exactly this rule in hardware.

The samples a settle keeps are one arrangement per sweep. Because each sweep starts from the one before, early sweeps still remember the coin flips they began with; the burn-in throws those away.

The schedule is geometric: it starts at ten times T and ends at a twentieth of it. Every puzzle on the puzzles page is solved by this one word.

For a picture the count is per pixel: how often each light was on is that pixel's grey. One sample is black and white; forty samples bring back the greys. That is the next section.

## (WAT DAT · THE HORSE, IN TRUE TIME)

The film player does the picture trick for every frame of a film: `play :img, frames: "dir/"`. Here it runs under **TRUE TIME RENDER**. A movie runs behind at its real pace, one frame every 500 ms, whatever this machine can do.

The field of 15,000 p-bits in front Settles toward the frame it was given. When its picture agrees with that frame 80%, it snaps to whatever frame the movie is at *now*. A fast machine draws many in-between pictures of each frame; a slow one draws few and skips frames; on both, the movie keeps time.

In machine-learning words the movie is a data stream on a fixed clock and the field is an anytime estimate, read out when it passes a quality bar and then re-aimed at the newest frame rather than the backlog. The clock is settle-see's `createTrueTime`. The film player page takes the per-frame Settling apart stage by stage, and the two strongest frame rows and three retraining runs are folded further down.

## (WAT DAT)

Six guests, two tables. Three pairs are old rivals and must sit apart; three pairs are friends and would like to sit together; and there is one small grudge. A guest is a thing: yes is table A, no is table B. Rivals push hard, friends pull gently, and the best seating is the calmest arrangement.

`anneal` finds it by starting hot, where every guest moves freely, then cooling slowly and keeping the calmest seating it passes through.

Energy -11: all three rival pairs are apart and so are the two with a grudge, while bo and eli, who are friends, sit at different tables. No seating does better; checking all 64 gives the same lowest energy. The puzzles page solves sudoku, graph colouring, max-cut and factoring the same way.

## (WAT DAT · DECISIONS AND STATE MACHINES)

Rain and a sprinkler can each wet the grass. Rain is unusual, the sprinkler a little less so, and nobody waters in the rain. You look outside and see that the grass is wet. How likely is it that it rained?

SETTLE answers by letting the three lights flip until they agree with each other, with the wet-grass light held on, and counting how often the rain light was on. A decision is a settle with a hold in it. Choose what you saw:

Holding the grass wet changes what calm looks like. The pull of 1.5 between rain and wet grass now rewards rain being on, and the pull of 1 does the same for the sprinkler. Both still lean toward off, so neither is certain. Either one explains the wet grass, so each ends up on about 64% of the time, and the push between them makes both at once less likely than it would be without it. With the grass held dry, rain almost never happens.

A state machine is the same Settling run over and over. The state is held, the machine settles, the answer is read, and that answer is held as the next state. Every step is one settle, so the machine can be as unsure as its coins are.

SDM EXPLORE draws Kanerva's memory as exactly this: every read is a step, and you can watch the state walk to a stored pattern, or refuse. SDMJEV, the magic 8 ball, is one pass of the same loop settled into an answer.

## (MEMORY)

The drawing stores a letter S so you can see it; the program beside it stores random patterns named :cat and :dog, and a line of text, in 512 things. The mechanism is the same.

Each recall lists how far the settled lights are from every stored pattern. +1.00 means they match :cat exactly; numbers near 0 mean unrelated. The text comes back letter for letter from a copy with 30% of its bits flipped. The SDMMEMORY page goes further, into Kanerva's sparse distributed memory.

## All the words on one screen (THE WHOLE LANGUAGE, IN WORDS)

Go deeper: the programming language (every statement, with the real output), the film player, memory, puzzles, learning and every result. The second half of this page, KANERVA, is the memory SETTLE remembers with.

## An address, a hard location, a write, a read, a noisy address (WAT DIS · FOR SDM)

Kanerva's memory stores long patterns of bits in a few thousand **hard locations**, each sitting at a random address in the space of all patterns. Five words make it, in the same shape as the six above. Each has its drawing, the lines of SETTLE's own `sdm` program that use it, and what the Rust `settle` binary printed when it ran.

In SETTLE a memory is a thing in the model: `sdm :s, word-size: 256, hard-locations: 2000` makes 256 address things and 2,000 hidden hard locations. A stored pattern is its own address: the memory is addressed by what it holds.

Each hard location keeps 256 small bit-counters, one per bit. The bit-counters live in the pulls between the hard location and the data things, so a hard location is a hidden thing in the settling machine and its bit-counters are weights.

Four patterns are written: three random ones named :cat, :dog and :owl, and a line of text. A text is written as its bits, so the same memory holds words and pictures. Nothing is stored whole anywhere; every pattern is spread over the locations it woke.

48 of 2,000 hard locations woke, two rounds of reading walked to a fixed point, and the answer matched :cat at +1.00. The numbers beside the other names are how far the answer is from them: near zero means unrelated.

At 40% noise the address wakes the wrong hard locations too, and the vote comes back with nothing clear: the closest name is :note at +0.62, which the program refuses to call a recall. The next section says where that line is.

## The Hamming ball, the vote, reading again, the critical distance, the soft read (HOW DAT · FOR SDM)

Five mechanisms do all the work. Each is one line of arithmetic on bits, and each has its drawing and its lines of code here.

The activation radius sets how many hard locations two patterns share. Two random patterns differ in about 128 bits, far outside the ball, so their hard locations barely overlap and the two writes do not mix. A noisy copy differs in fewer, so it still shares most of them.

A vote is a majority, and a majority is a hard cut. In SETTLE's terms the tally is the input I to a coin that is cold enough to follow it every time. Warm it up and the read becomes the soft read below.

Pure noise walked three rounds and fell into :cat: with nothing written near a random address, whichever stored pattern has the most hard locations in reach wins the vote, and the next round pulls the answer the rest of the way in.

The :owl read at 40% noise and the :zebra read (never written, so there is nothing to converge to) both stop outside the critical distance, and the program says so rather than naming a pattern. SDM EXPLORE draws this distance live.

`softness` blurs the cut-off of the ball and `fire` sets what fraction of locations wake; `attend` computes the attention limit outside the sampler, so the two can be compared. The soft memory is the one that settles: its hard locations are p-bits like everything else.

## Letters healed, a text back, too far, never written, keys (WAT DAT · FOR SDM)

The same mechanism brings a text back letter for letter from a copy with 15% of its bits flipped. The SDMMEMORY page runs this on words you type: SDMMEMORY.

Pure noise falls into the nearest valley (:cat), and that is honest too: the program reports which pattern it fell into and how far it was. SDM REFUSE, on the results page, measured how often each case is told apart.

SDMCHAT is that model, live in your browser; the poem lab has it recite a whole poem; SDMJEV reads one answer out of its vector space. KANERVA is the toolbox, with the dollar of Mexico and king and queen in plain words.

## Kanerva, and the two his memory stands between (WHO DIS · FOR SDM)

Sparse distributed memory is Pentti Kanerva's (1988). It stands between Hopfield's network, where every pattern is a calm arrangement of the whole machine, and attention, where every stored row is weighted by how near it is. The credits page has the papers.

## A memory the machine can settle into (HOW IT MEETS SETTLE)

**Three readings of one memory.** Kanerva's read is a vote; the read by the pulls is a settle of the data things with the locations held; the soft read warms the coins. All three are the tanh rule at a different temperature, which is why one language holds them. SDM EXPLORE draws the memory as a state diagram you operate.
